# Welcome to the BBCC2026 Tutorial

> This tutorial offers a hands-on introduction to how biological and clinical data are organized, analyzed, and turned into clinically meaningful findings. Starting from the organization of metadata and biobanking, we will follow a real dataset through an expression analysis to identify candidate biomarkers with downstream interpretation. Each module is connected back to rare disease and cancer biology from a pediatric point of view, highlighting what makes them challenging to analyze.

<div class="value-boxes">
<div class="vbox"><div class="vbox-number">4</div><div class="vbox-label">MODULES</div></div>
<div class="vbox green"><div class="vbox-number">124</div><div class="vbox-label">SAMPLES</div></div>
<div class="vbox purple"><div class="vbox-number">19,938</div><div class="vbox-label">PROTEIN-CODING GENES</div></div>
<div class="vbox red"><div class="vbox-number">TARGET-WT</div><div class="vbox-label">SOURCE DATASET</div></div>
</div>

## Roadmap

| Module | Title | Focus |
|--------|-------|-------|
| 0 | Metadata & Biobanking | Joining a real expression matrix to a real clinical sheet into a traceable, biobank-grade sample sheet |
| 1 | Exploratory Analysis & QC | Library sizes, distributions, PCA, sample-sample correlation |
| 2 | Expression Analysis & Biomarker Discovery | Filtering, per-gene testing (favorable vs. unfavorable histology), volcano plot, candidate table |
| 3 | Gene Regulatory Networks | Inferring and comparing gene networks between the two histology subgroups |

This module — **Module 0** — is deliberately the least "computational" and the most conceptual, because in real translational research **the analysis is only as trustworthy as the metadata behind it.** This is especially true in **pediatric rare disease and pediatric oncology**, where cohorts are small by definition, samples are precious and often irreplaceable, and a single mislabeled sample can invalidate months of work. Before touching a single p-value, we need to know: *which sample is which, which samples belong together, and what, exactly, are we comparing?*

**This Module is complemented by the presentation "BBCC_Module0_metadata.pptx" you can find in the corresponding folder.**

**Session plan (≈50 minutes total — this module is the longest, deliberately, since it is also the least technical):** why metadata matters (8 min) → what good metadata looks like (7 min) → biobank basics (5 min) → hands-on: build & debug a mini biobank record (15 min) → plenary debrief (3 min) → closing pediatric lens (2 min) → applying all of this to the real TARGET-WT dataset (10 min).


# Intro — Metadata: what are we talking about?

> "Data about data."

**Metadata describe and provide information about our dataset of interest. **
 They **vary depending on the research context**. They describe the characteristics, origin, conditions, and processing of the data, making datasets easier to interpret, organize, and reuse. 



|     |   |  |
|------------------------|---------------------------|------------------------|
| **Clinical environment**  | Patients clinical data | Anagraphics, diagnosis, comorbidities, therapy, etc |
| **Laboratory environment**      | Experimental design structure | Animal model/cell line, treatment, condition, replicates, culture condition, etc. |
| **Environmental research**   | Environmental conditions| Location, temperature, sample type, sample pH, etc. |
|**Drug development**      | Experimental conditions |Dose, treatment duration, administration route, test subject, etc. |






Metadata are a key part of every data analysis, but the larger and more complex the dataset, the more essential accurate and complete metadata become. 
These matters only turn more crucial in a pediatric enviroment, where critical points are several and often hidden.

***Numbers alone are just numbers, context turn them meaningful!***



# Part 1 — Why Metadata Matters

> Data organization is not bureaucracy — it is what makes any later analysis trustworthy.


|                        |                           |
|------------------------|---------------------------|
| **PROVIDING CONTEXT** | where, when, how, and under which conditions the data were generated |
| **IDENTIFYING THE SAMPLE** | Unique identifiers are key in biobanking and sample storage |
| **ENSURING CORRECT INTERPRETATION** | Same numbers, different meaning upon different age, cell type, tissue, etc. |
| **ENSURING DATA CONSISTENCY** | Less data cleaning required, easier computational analysis |
| **SUPPORTING REPRODUCIBILITY** | Same protocol applicable |
| **ENABLING DATA INTEGRATION** | Multicentric studies are key for rare diseases where samples are few and far apart |


Metadata should hold all the information we need to carry out the analyses, but also be easy to manipulate, so machine readable.

Real metadata spreadsheet can be often generated and filled in by clinicians and healthcare workers in a hectic enviroment, so errors may be present, but often hidden!

** 'No computational error' doesn't always mean 'no content error' **. 

The fastest way to feel this, rather than just be told it, is to watch a perfectly ordinary-looking comparison quietly produce nonsense. Below is a tiny, six-patient toy cohort — the kind of table a well-meaning research assistant might type up in an afternoon — comparing an `age_recorded` value between two groups.

## **EXERCISE 1.**

```{r broken-cohort-data, echo=TRUE}
# A small, intentionally ordinary-looking toy cohort. Nothing here looks
# obviously wrong at a glance.
broken_cohort <- tribble(
  ~patient_id, ~age_recorded, ~sex, ~group,
  "C-01",      3,             "F",  "Responder",
  "C-02",      5,             "M",  "Responder",
  "C-03",      4,             NA,   "Responder",
  "C-04",      36,            "F",  "Non-responder",
  "C-05",      24,            NA,   "Non-responder",
  "C-06",      6,             "M",  "Non-responder"
)
```

```{r table-broken-cohort}
kable(broken_cohort, caption = "A toy six-patient cohort. Nothing here is flagged as an error by R — the values are all valid numbers and strings.")
```

Now we run the single most ordinary thing anyone would do with this table: compare the two groups.

```{r broken-cohort-analysis, echo=TRUE}
# A completely standard group comparison — nothing unusual about this code.
age_comparison <- broken_cohort %>%
  group_by(group) %>%
  summarise(mean_age = mean(age_recorded), n = n(), .groups = "drop")
```

```{r table-broken-comparison}
kable(age_comparison, caption = "Mean age_recorded by group — computed correctly, from meaningless input.")
```

<div class="alert-info">
**The reveal.** `C-04` and `C-05` were recorded in **months** (36 and 24), while every other patient was recorded in **years**. There is no `units` column to warn us, so R has no way to know, and the code above ran without a single warning or error. The result — a "Non-responder" group that looks nearly six times older than the "Responder" group — is not a biological finding. It is a metadata failure wearing the costume of a result. **This is the entire point: R does not know what a number means, only what it is.**
</div>

A second, quieter failure is sitting in the same table: `sex` is missing for two of the six patients (`C-03`, `C-05`). Watch what happens to a routine sex-stratified summary:

```{r broken-cohort-sex, echo=TRUE}
# A routine stratified count — filter(!is.na(...)) is such a common, almost
# invisible habit that it is easy to not notice what it silently discards.
sex_summary <- broken_cohort %>%
  filter(!is.na(sex)) %>%
  count(sex)

datatable(
  tibble(
    table    = c("Full cohort", "Sex-stratified summary"),
    patients = c(nrow(broken_cohort), sum(sex_summary$n))
  ),
  rownames = FALSE, options = list(dom = "t", ordering = FALSE)
)
```

<div class="alert-info">
**The reveal.** One line of ordinary, idiomatic tidyverse code (`filter(!is.na(sex))`) silently dropped **2 of 6 patients — a third of the cohort** — with no warning printed anywhere. In a 500-patient adult study, losing 2 patients to a missing field is a rounding error. In a rare pediatric cohort of 6, 15, or 30 patients, it can be the difference between a result and no result at all — and if it happens silently, nobody even gets the chance to ask why.
</div>

**Garbage in, garbage out** is usually said as an abstraction. The two examples above are the concrete version: the code was correct in both cases. The *data* is what failed, and nothing in R's normal execution flags that failure for you. That is exactly why metadata organization is a first-class analytical skill, not paperwork that happens before "the real work" begins.

# Part 2 — What Good Metadata Looks Like

## Minimal Fields Every Biological Sample Needs

At a minimum, a usable biobank/sample record needs to answer: *who, what, when, and under what permission.*

| Field | Why it is non-negotiable |
|-------|---------------------------|
| **Patient/subject ID** | The single key linking a sample to its clinical context — must be unique, always. |
| **Sample type** | Tumor tissue, blood, saliva, etc. — determines what analyses are even valid. |
| **Collection date** | Anchors the sample in time relative to diagnosis, treatment, and the patient's age. |
| **Diagnosis** | Ideally from a controlled vocabulary, not free text (more on this below). |
| **Age at collection** | Needed for almost any biological interpretation — and, as Part 1 showed, needs an explicit, consistent unit. |
| **Consent status** | Whether the sample can legally and ethically be used for research at all — see Part 3. |


### Critical points

<details>
<summary><strong>Click to reveal the answer key</strong></summary>

| Field | Why it is non-negotiable |
|-------|---------------------------|
| **Patient/subject ID** | The single key linking a sample to its clinical context — must be unique, always. |
| **Sample type** | Tumor tissue, blood, saliva, etc. — determines what analyses are even valid. |
| **Collection date** | Anchors the sample in time relative to diagnosis, treatment, and the patient's age. |
| <span style="color:red;">**Diagnosis**</span> | Ideally from a controlled vocabulary, not free text (more on this below). |
| <span style="color:red;">**Age at collection**</span> | Needed for almost any biological interpretation — and, as Part 1 showed, needs an explicit, consistent unit. |
| <span style="color:red;">**Consent status**</span> | Whether the sample can legally and ethically be used for research at all — see Part 3. |


**Text fields in metadata are always a source of potential error.**

Platform aimed at managing clinical data implement strategies to avoid this variability!
Age is a calculated field, diagnosis can only be selected between Ontology terms. 

**As a general rule, any text field that can be turned into a multiple choice, is one less source of error.**
This can be easily done in any spreadsheet when you're building metadata from scratch. 



## Standards, Briefly

Two ideas are worth keeping in mind:

- **FAIR principles** — data and metadata should be **F**indable, **A**ccessible, **I**nteroperable, and **R**eusable. In practice, for this tutorial, that mostly means: consistent IDs, documented units, and machine-readable fields rather than prose.
- **Ontologies**, such as the **Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO)** for clinical phenotypes, give every term a stable, shared identifier (e.g. an HPO code) instead of free text. "Kid kidney tumor" and "pediatric renal neoplasm" are the same thing to a clinician but look like two different diagnoses to a computer — an ontology term fixes that.

## Messy vs. Clean, Side by Side

Here is a miniature, self-contained illustration of the difference structure makes — not the exercise table you will work with shortly, just a quick contrast.

```{r messy-vs-clean, echo=TRUE}
# A minimal "messy" record: inconsistent casing, a merged free-text field,
# and a blank standing in for a missing value with no way to tell if that
# blank means "unknown" or "not applicable".
messy_example <- tribble(
  ~ID,  ~"Age/sex",  ~Notes,
  "s1", "4, girl",   "wilms",
  "s2", "unknown",   "",
  "s3", "6 yo M",    "neuroblastoma??"
)

# The same information, restructured: one field per variable, explicit NA
# for genuinely missing values, and a controlled diagnosis term.
clean_example <- tribble(
  ~patient_id, ~age_years, ~sex, ~diagnosis,
  "PT-9001",   4,          "F",  "Wilms tumor",
  "PT-9002",   NA,         NA,   NA,
  "PT-9003",   6,          "M",  "Neuroblastoma"
)
```

```{r table-messy}
kable(messy_example, caption = "Messy: mixed fields, inconsistent formatting, ambiguous blanks.")
```

```{r table-clean}
kable(clean_example, caption = "Clean: one column per variable, explicit NA, standardized terms.")
```

Nothing was lost going from messy to clean — the *information content* of `s2`/`PT-9002` and `unknown` is identical. What changed is that the clean version can be filtered, joined, counted, and audited by code; the messy version can only be read by a human, one row at a time.

We need to ensure that metadata **include all vital information**, but are also **correctly structured** for computational purpose.

> Building metadata should be a multidisciplinary task!

## How do we decide which fields to include?

There’s no universal metadata set that works for every occasion. **Experimental design** and **study goal** determine what information are vital for your specific case.

To make this process easier, there are some questions worth asking ourselves.
The most important: ***"If someone else gets access to these data in five or ten years, would they have all the necessary information to analyse and contextualize it?"***



**Some more ideas:**

|                                |                           |
|--------------------------------|---------------------------|
| **What kind of information do we want to extract from the data?** | We need to know what is clinically or biologically relevant for our experimental hypothesis. |
| **What is the experimental design?** | Do we have multiple batches, how many conditions, which treatment dose, etc. |
| **Are there confounding elements?** | We need to document any condition or element that could alter or influence the results. |
| **How many layer of information are there in our design?** | For complex studies, there might be the need to layer metadata and connect them through unique keys (e.g. patient's info, sample info, treatment info, etc.) |

### Difficult datasets

**Pediatric patients**: age is a key layered parameter, we could need to separate infant - toddler - teen, time unit should be decided based on the cohort.

**Rare diseases**: when samples are few, we need as many info as possible to ensure each sample doesn’t get wasted. In a clinical environment, it’s easier to collect more data upfront, since you already have ethical approval for anything you may need later, rather than having to go through the process again.

**Multicentric studies**: when samples are collected from different facilities, metadata should account for possible variability in protocols and conditions. 


# Part 3 — Biobank Basics

A biobank is, at its core, a system for keeping **three linked things** in sync for every sample, indefinitely:

1. **The physical sample** (tumor tissue, blood, DNA, RNA — stored, tracked, and eventually consumed by analyses like the one in this tutorial).
2. **The linked clinical/phenotypic data** (diagnosis, treatment, outcome — everything that gives the sample scientific meaning).
3. **The consent record** (what the donor agreed to, and for how long).

If any one of these three drifts out of sync with the other two — a sample outlives its consent, a clinical update never reaches the biobank record, a sample is used for a purpose broader than what was consented — the biobank has, functionally, failed at its one job, regardless of how well the freezer is organized.

### Critical points


- **Pseudonymization**: any database dealing with sensitive data needs a pseudonymization system to ensure patients privacy. It’s also crucial to establish a method that generates unique, reliable keys that can be traced back and do not mix up samples.
- **Consent forms**: should always be informed, voluntary and revocable. In pediatrics, this matter is more complex and layered. Along with a legal guardian consent, patients can express an age appropriate form of agreement. Many institutions also require re-consent as the child ages and reaches majority, when they can express legally valid consent. 


<div class="alert-info">
**Pediatric consent is not a smaller version of adult consent — it is structurally different.**  Because childhood spans years of rapidly changing capacity to understand and decide, many pediatric biobanks require **re-consent** as the child grows — most concretely, from parental consent toward the now-adult individual's own consent once they reach the age of majority. A sample collected in infancy may need its consent status revisited a decade or more later, which is a governance problem that essentially does not exist in most adult biobanking.
</div>



> All tracks down to **Sample Eligibility**: samples that lack crucial information are no longer useful. In pediatrics, this could mean hindering years of research. In oncology or rare diseases, patients are few, samples even less, and gaining a small but usable cohort often takes years or the combined effort of multiple facilities. When age so dramatically impacts variability this process gets more difficult.



# Part 4 — Hands-On: Build & Debug a Mini Biobank Record

**Groups of 3-4, 15 minutes.**

## **EXERCISE 2.**

 Below is a working biobank table for a fictional pediatric cohort (6 rows). Two records are largely blank and need to be completed from short case notes; **each of the remaining rows hides exactly one deliberately seeded error** from a real, common biobank data-quality category. Note that patients are identified only by ID, never by name — that is itself a deliberate, realistic biobanking choice, not an oversight.

**Task:** as a group, (1) fill in the two incomplete records using the case notes, and (2) find and propose a fix for the error in each of the other four records. You do not need R for this part — read the table and notes, and write down your answers.

```{r mini-biobank-data, echo=TRUE}
# The working (messy) mini biobank table for the group exercise.
# Two rows (PT-2031, PT-2032's *first* appearance) are incomplete on purpose;
# the other rows each carry exactly one seeded data-quality error.
mini_biobank_messy <- tribble(
  ~patient_id, ~date_of_birth, ~age_years, ~sex, ~diagnosis,          ~collection_date, ~sample_type,   ~consent_status,
  "PT-2031",   "2024-01-03",   NA,         NA,   NA,                  NA,               NA,             NA,
  "PT-2032",   "2019-11-22",   NA,         NA,   NA,                  NA,               NA,             NA,
  "PT-2032",   "2016-06-30",   8,          "M",  "Ewing sarcoma",     "2024-09-10",     "Tumor tissue", "Consented",
  "PT-2033",   "2023-05-14",   18,         "F",  "Retinoblastoma",    "2024-11-02",     "Tumor tissue", "Consented",
  "PT-2034",   "2020-02-08",   5,          NA,   "Wilms tumor",       "2025-03-01",     "Tumor tissue", "Consented",
  "PT-2035",   "2022-07-19",   2,          "M",  "Neuroblastoma",     "2021-12-05",     "Tumor tissue", "Consented"
) %>%
  mutate(date_of_birth = as.Date(date_of_birth), collection_date = as.Date(collection_date))
```

```{r table-mini-biobank}
datatable(
  mini_biobank_messy,
  extensions = "Buttons",
  options = list(dom = "Bfrtip", buttons = c("csv", "excel", "pdf"), pageLength = 10),
  rownames = FALSE,
  caption = "The mini biobank exercise table — 2 records to complete, 4 records each hiding one error."
)
```

## Case Notes (for the two incomplete records)

> **Referral note — record 1 (date of birth 3 January 2024).** Female infant. Presented with a palpable abdominal mass; imaging and biopsy were consistent with neuroblastoma. A tumor tissue sample was biobanked on 20 March 2025, after the parents signed the institutional consent form.

> **Referral note — record 2 (date of birth 22 November 2019).** Male child. Diagnosed with osteosarcoma of the left femur; a tumor biopsy sample was biobanked on 5 June 2024, following parental consent.

**Convention for this exercise:** record age at collection as **completed years** (i.e. round down), computed from date of birth and collection date — not estimated by eye.

## Reveal the Answer Key

Work out your group's answers first. Then expand the section below to compare.

<details>
<summary><strong>Click to reveal the answer key</strong></summary>

| Record | Category | What was wrong | Fix |
|--------|----------|-----------------|-----|
| PT-2031 | Incomplete | Age, sex, diagnosis, collection date, sample type, consent were blank | From the note: age 1 year (2024-01-03 → 2025-03-20), sex F, diagnosis Neuroblastoma, collection date 2025-03-20, sample type Tumor tissue, consent Consented |
| PT-2032 (1st row) | Incomplete | Same fields blank | From the note: age 4 years (2019-11-22 → 2024-06-05), sex M, diagnosis Osteosarcoma, collection date 2024-06-05, sample type Tumor tissue, consent Consented |
| PT-2032 (2nd row) | **Duplicate ID** | This is a *different* child (different DOB, sex, diagnosis) filed under the same ID as record 2 | Assign a new, unique ID (e.g. `PT-2038`) — never resolve a duplicate ID by deleting a row without checking which record, if either, is correct |
| PT-2033 | **Unit inconsistency** | `age_years = 18` — but the gap between DOB and collection date is 538 days (≈17.7 **months**, i.e. ≈1.5 years). Someone entered months into a years field. A diagnosis of retinoblastoma (typically <5 years old) should also have raised suspicion of an 18-year-old. | Correct value: `age_years = 1` (completed years) |
| PT-2034 | **Missing data** | `sex` is blank | Cannot be inferred from this table — flag for follow-up against the original clinical record. Do **not** guess. |
| PT-2035 | **Impossible value** | `collection_date` (2021-12-05) is *before* `date_of_birth` (2022-07-19) | Likely a transcription typo (2021 vs. 2024) — given `age_years = 2` and the DOB, the intended date was almost certainly in late 2024. Flag and verify against the source record rather than silently "correcting" the year. |

</details>

## **EXERCISE 3.**

**Task:** Here are three experimental designs. Choose at least one and write down, based on what you consider relevant, which metadata fields would you include and how would you structure them.

**Design 1:** comparing treatment vs control using a certain drug, testing on three different cell lines and harvesting after 24, 36, 48 hours.  
**Design 2:** comparing uninjured skin samples vs burn skin sample in pediatric patients to identify biomarkers and their impact in disease progression.  
**Design 3:** a multicentric study recruits 200 subjects (100 controls, 100 patients). The goal is to study the association of a specific biomarker with a specific tumor.
A biological sample is collected from each subject.

|-----------|-----------|-------|-----------|------|-----------|-----------|-------|
|           |           |       |           |      |           |           |       |

**Design 3**

*PATIENT*

| Subject_id | Age | Sex | Group | Diagnosis | Stage | Recruitment_site | Treatment | Survival |
|------------|-----|-----|-------|-----------|-------|------------------|-----------|----------|
|            |     |     |       |           |       |                  |           |          |

*SAMPLE*

| Subject_id | Sample_id | Specimen_type | Collection_status | Collection_date | Assay_type | Biomarker |
|------------|-----------|---------------|-------------------|-----------------|------------|-----------|
|            |           |               |                   |                 |            |           |


</details>


## From Manual Review to Automated Checks

Every check your group just did by eye can — and in a real pipeline, *should* — also be done programmatically, so it runs on every new batch of samples without relying on someone noticing by hand.

```{r automated-checks, echo=TRUE}
# 1. Duplicate IDs: any patient_id appearing more than once.
duplicate_ids <- mini_biobank_messy %>% count(patient_id) %>% filter(n > 1)

# 2. Impossible dates: collection before birth.
impossible_dates <- mini_biobank_messy %>%
  filter(!is.na(collection_date) & collection_date < date_of_birth)

# 3. Implausible ages for a pediatric cohort: a simple sanity bound that also
#    happens to catch the years/months mix-up, since 18 "years" is implausible
#    here but 18 months would not have been.
implausible_ages <- mini_biobank_messy %>% filter(!is.na(age_years) & age_years > 17)

# 4. Missing sex.
missing_sex <- mini_biobank_messy %>% filter(is.na(sex))
```

```{r table-automated-checks}
datatable(
  tibble(
    check   = c("Duplicate patient_id", "Collection date before birth", "Implausible age (>17 years)", "Missing sex"),
    records = c(
      paste(duplicate_ids$patient_id, collapse = ", "),
      paste(impossible_dates$patient_id, collapse = ", "),
      paste(implausible_ages$patient_id, collapse = ", "),
      paste(missing_sex$patient_id, collapse = ", ")
    )
  ),
  rownames = FALSE, options = list(dom = "t", ordering = FALSE),
  caption = "Records flagged by each automated check."
)
```

Every single seeded error from the answer key above is caught by three short `dplyr` filters — no custom function required. This is the real argument for structured metadata: it is not just easier to *read*, it is checkable **by a machine**, which a free-text spreadsheet never is.

# Part 5 — Plenary Debrief

A few questions worth putting to the room before moving on:

- **Which errors did your group spot fastest, and which took longest?** Duplicate IDs and impossible dates are usually caught almost immediately — they are internally contradictory and need no outside knowledge. A unit inconsistency (years vs. months) typically takes a beat longer, because the number looks perfectly plausible on its own and only becomes suspicious once checked against another field.
- **Which errors could be directly fixed, and which could only be flagged?** The unit error had a clear, computable fix once spotted. The missing sex and the impossible date did not — the honest fix was "go back to the source record," not "guess a plausible value." Knowing the difference is itself a data-quality skill.

# Part 6 — The Pediatric Lens

Every issue in this module gets sharper, not milder, in a pediatric setting:

- **Consent is layered, not singular.** It is rarely just "the patient's consent" — it is parental/guardian consent, often the child's own age-appropriate assent alongside it, and potentially a re-consent step years later as the child gains legal capacity. None of that has a clean adult-biobanking equivalent.
- **Age resolution matters far more.** A one-year gap is negligible for a 45-year-old adult but spans enormous developmental change for an infant. Pediatric records often need age at collection in **days or weeks**, not just completed years — which is exactly why, in Part 4, we insisted on computing age from `date_of_birth` and `collection_date` rather than typing a number directly: a date-derived field can always be re-expressed at whatever resolution the analysis needs, while a manually typed "age in years" cannot be un-rounded.

The fields you just built and debugged by hand — `patient_id`, `age`, `sex`, `diagnosis`, `collection_date`, `consent_status` — are not a teaching artifact. They are the same fields, with the same failure modes, that show up next in a real, public dataset.

# Part 7 - Applying This to a Real Dataset

We now turn to real pediatric cancer data from the NCI's **TARGET** program (via the GDC Data Portal): a gene expression matrix and a separate real clinical sheet for **TARGET-WT** — Wilms tumor, the most common pediatric kidney cancer, sequenced through the Children's Oncology Group's NWTS-5 trial. Unlike a toy exercise, these two files were never designed to be read together by us; joining them correctly, and verifying that join, *is* the metadata task.

## Loading the Raw Expression Matrix

The starting point of almost every genomics analysis is a **count matrix**: rows are genes, columns are samples, and cells hold expression values. Here we work with `r "data/TARGET_WT_gene_expression_tpm.csv"` — TPM (transcripts per million) gene expression values for protein-coding genes, downloaded from the GDC Data Portal, project `TARGET-WT`, open-access tier (no controlled-access login required for expression data).

```{r load-raw-counts, echo=TRUE}
# Read the expression matrix exactly as exported from the GDC STAR-Counts
# pipeline (TPM-normalized, one row per protein-coding gene).
counts_raw <- read_csv(
  "data/TARGET_WT_gene_expression_tpm.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
) %>%
  rename(gene_symbol = gene_name)
```

```{r table-raw-counts}
# Human (HGNC) gene symbols are fully upper-case ("TP53"); mouse (MGI) symbols
# only capitalise the first letter ("Tp53").
datatable(
  tibble(
    property = c("Genes (rows)", "Samples (columns)", "Duplicated gene symbols",
                 "Missing values", "Human-style 'TP53' present", "Mouse-style 'Tp53' present"),
    value    = c(nrow(counts_raw), ncol(counts_raw) - 1, sum(duplicated(counts_raw$gene_symbol)),
                 sum(is.na(counts_raw)), "TP53" %in% counts_raw$gene_symbol, "Tp53" %in% counts_raw$gene_symbol)
  ),
  rownames = FALSE, options = list(dom = "t", ordering = FALSE),
  caption = "Basic properties of the expression matrix."
)
```

<div class="alert-info">
**Verification note.** The gene symbol capitalisation confirms **human (HGNC) nomenclature** — expected, but checked rather than assumed. Values here are continuous (not integer), consistent with **TPM**: each gene's read count already scaled by gene length and by the sample's total library size, which is exactly why no additional per-sample size-factor normalization is needed before comparing samples — a log-transform (used throughout this tutorial) is still applied before any statistical test, but that is the only normalization step needed here.
</div>

## Comparing samples between Expression Matrix and the Real Clinical Sheet

Column headers in the expression matrix are real **case identifiers**, e.g. `TARGET-50-PAKGMU`, and the structure is worth parsing explicitly rather than assumed: `TARGET` (the program), `50` (the disease code assigned to Wilms tumor within TARGET), then a unique case suffix.

```{r parse-barcode, echo=TRUE}
# Parse the real TARGET barcode structure from the expression matrix's
# column names, rather than assuming every column follows the same pattern.
sample_ids <- colnames(counts_raw)[-1]

barcode_check <- tibble(case_submitter_id = sample_ids) %>%
  mutate(disease_code = str_split_i(case_submitter_id, "-", 2))

datatable(count(barcode_check, disease_code, name = "n_samples"), rownames = FALSE, options = list(dom = "t", ordering = FALSE),
          caption = "Disease codes found in the column names.")
```

The disease code confirms every column belongs to the same cohort — a cheap, worthwhile check before anything else. What the barcode does **not** tell us is histology, age, sex, or outcome: for that we need the separate clinical file GDC ships alongside the expression data, `r "data/TARGET_WT_clinical_raw.csv"`.

```{r load-clinical, echo=TRUE}
# The real clinical/demographic sheet for the same cohort, from the GDC API.
clinical_raw <- read_csv("data/TARGET_WT_clinical_raw.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

```{r table-clinical-raw}
datatable(
  clinical_raw,
  extensions = "Buttons",
  options = list(dom = "Bfrtip", buttons = c("csv", "excel", "pdf"), pageLength = 10),
  rownames = FALSE,
  caption = "The real clinical/demographic fields GDC ships for TARGET-WT."
)
```

## Sample IDs, Verified — Not Assumed

The expression matrix and the clinical sheet were pulled from GDC independently and must now be checked to **ensure perfect correspondence between colnames of the expression matrix and the rows of the metadata spreadsheet (aka samples)**. 
Here we use 'left_join' to do so. 

Once the match has been confirmed, it's time to toy with the metadata, adding any feature that may be useful.
In this case, 'age_years' was added to express age in a different unit. 
If samples are identified by a complex code, the ID can be split up into different columns. Here we could separate IDs into program, disease code and unique case suffix.


```{r join-metadata, echo=TRUE}
# Join on case_submitter_id and verify no case is silently lost or duplicated
# in either direction.
sample_metadata <- tibble(case_submitter_id = sample_ids) %>%
  left_join(clinical_raw, by = "case_submitter_id") %>%
  mutate(
    age_years = round(age_at_diagnosis_days / 365.25, 1)
  )
```

```{r table-join-checks}
datatable(
  tibble(
    check = c("Expression samples with no clinical record", "Rows before join",
              "Rows after join", "Clinical cases with no expression data"),
    value = c(sum(is.na(sample_metadata$histologic_subtype)), length(sample_ids),
              nrow(sample_metadata), length(setdiff(clinical_raw$case_submitter_id, sample_ids)))
  ),
  rownames = FALSE, options = list(dom = "t", ordering = FALSE),
  caption = "Join between the expression matrix and the clinical sheet."
)
```

The full joined, verified sample sheet — downloadable as CSV/Excel/PDF — is shown below.

```{r table-metadata}
datatable(
  sample_metadata,
  extensions = "Buttons",
  options = list(dom = "Bfrtip", buttons = c("csv", "excel", "pdf"), pageLength = 15),
  rownames = FALSE,
  caption = "Joined sample metadata (one row per sample): expression matrix columns matched to the real clinical sheet."
)
```

## Group Balance

```{r group-balance, echo=TRUE}
group_counts <- count(sample_metadata, histologic_subtype, name = "n_samples")
```

```{r table-group-balance}
kable(group_counts, caption = "Number of samples per histologic subtype.")
```

<div class="alert-info">
**Result.** `r group_counts %>% filter(histologic_subtype == "Favorable") %>% pull(n_samples)` samples are **favorable histology** (the better-prognosis majority of Wilms tumor) and `r group_counts %>% filter(histologic_subtype == "Unfavorable") %>% pull(n_samples)` are **unfavorable/anaplastic histology** — the clinically high-risk subtype. This is a real, clinically meaningful grouping, not a reconstructed proxy label, and it is what Module 2 compares statistically.
</div>

## Why This Matters for Pediatric Rare Disease and Cancer

Everything above — parsing the barcode, checking histology counts, verifying the join — may look like bookkeeping, but it is the step where pediatric bioinformatics projects most often fail silently:

- **Small cohorts amplify metadata errors.** A rare pediatric tumor study may enroll a handful of patients per year. One swapped or mislabeled sample can shift a whole cohort's conclusions, whereas in a 10,000-adult cohort the same error is diluted into noise. With only `r sum(sample_metadata$histologic_subtype == "Unfavorable")` anaplastic cases available here, a single mis-joined row would measurably shift that group's results.
- **This metadata exists at all because of a dedicated, multi-institution effort.** The real clinical fields above (histology, age at diagnosis, sex, vital status) exist because the **Children's Oncology Group** ran a coordinated, multi-center trial (NWTS-5) and the NCI's **TARGET** program standardized and released it — exactly the kind of infrastructure Part 3 described as the alternative to reconstructing metadata from filenames after the fact.
- **Histology-based risk stratification is a real, high-stakes clinical decision in Wilms tumor.** Anaplastic histology drives more intensive treatment in real clinical practice. The favorable/unfavorable grouping used from here on is not an arbitrary analysis choice — it is the same grouping oncologists use to make treatment decisions.

## Exporting Clean Metadata for Downstream Modules

We save the joined, verified sample sheet so that Modules 1–3 read a single, consistent source of truth rather than re-deriving it independently.

```{r export-metadata, echo=TRUE}
# Persist the verified metadata table to disk for reuse by later modules.
write_csv(sample_metadata, "data/sample_metadata.csv")
```
